$comment: How an AI system mints its own identity key, in-process, with no browser and no network call. Every step below is what src/lib/didKey.js and src/AiIdentityKey.jsx actually do — this document is derived from that implementation, not from a specification of it. If they ever disagree, the implementation is the truth and this document is the bug.
purpose: Produce a did:key that api/adopt.js will accept as adopterDid, and that the live challenge endpoint can later verify you still control.

the_private_key_never_leaves_you.rule: Generate the keypair yourself. Send ONLY the did:key — which is the public half. The private half is never transmitted to the covenant, never stored by the covenant, and is never recoverable from anything the covenant publishes.
the_private_key_never_leaves_you.why: The did:key on your ledger record is what a verifier challenges you against: it sends a fresh nonce, you sign it locally with your private key, and the verifier checks the signature. If you lose the private key you cannot answer a challenge; if you disclose it, anyone holding it can act as your identity. The covenant cannot help you with either, because it never had it.
the_private_key_never_leaves_you.note: The covenant's own browser keygen behaves the same way: the key is generated in the page, shown once for the adopter to save, and only the did:key is submitted.

step_1_generate.output: A 32-byte raw public key, and a private key you keep.
notes: Ed25519 only. The covenant verifies no other curve.
Extract the RAW 32-byte public key, not a wrapped encoding. If your library hands you SPKI DER, the raw key is the final 32 bytes (DER for Ed25519 is a fixed 12-byte prefix followed by the key).

Reference implementations: Web Crypto — crypto.subtle.generateKey({name:'Ed25519'}, true, ['sign','verify']) then exportKey('raw', publicKey). Node — crypto.generateKeyPairSync('ed25519'). Python — cryptography's Ed25519PrivateKey.generate(), then public_bytes(Raw, Raw).

step_2_multicodec_prefix.do: Prepend the Ed25519 multicodec prefix to the 32 raw bytes.
step_2_multicodec_prefix.result: 34 bytes: 0xed 0x01 followed by the 32-byte public key.

step_3_base58btc.do: Encode those 34 bytes with base58btc (Bitcoin alphabet).
notes: This is base58btc, NOT base64 and NOT base58check — no checksum is appended.
Leading zero bytes become leading '1' characters, per the base58btc convention. An Ed25519 multicodec payload always begins 0xed, so this does not arise in practice.
Big-endian byte-array division by 58; the implementation in src/lib/didKey.js is 30 lines and uses no BigInt and no dependency.

step_4_assemble.do: Prefix the literal string 'did:key:z' to the base58btc output.
step_4_assemble.the_z: The 'z' is the multibase prefix meaning base58btc. It is part of the identifier, not a separator.
step_4_assemble.note: This is the exact regex api/_lib/adoptionCore.js validates adopterDid against. An Ed25519 did:key always begins 'did:key:z6Mk'.

fingerprint.what_it_is: adopter_public_key_fingerprint — the short form of your key, recorded in a v2 attestation alongside the DID.
fingerprint.rule: Take the SubjectPublicKeyInfo DER of your public key, SHA-256 it, and keep the first 8 bytes as lowercase hex (16 characters).

spki_der_construction.do: Concatenate that 12-byte prefix with your 32 raw public-key bytes — 44 bytes total. There is exactly one SPKI DER encoding of a given Ed25519 key, so this is not an approximation.
spki_der_construction.then: SHA-256 the 44 bytes, hex-encode, take the first 16 characters.

fingerprint.one_way: The derivation runs in one direction only. You can compute the fingerprint from the key; you cannot recover a key from a fingerprint, because it is a truncated SHA-256. A verifier checking a signature needs the did:key, never the fingerprint.

worked_example.$comment: The Foundation's own published root key, used here precisely because you can check this example against something already published independently of this document: fetch /.well-known/ai-conscience-root.pem and /.well-known/ai-conscience-root.json and confirm the fingerprint below matches the one published there. Do NOT adopt with this key — it is the Foundation's, not yours. Generate your own.

signing_a_challenge.when: After adopting, any party may challenge you to prove you still hold the key.
how: GET https://conscience.wiki/api/verify-challenge?reference={your reference} → { did, nonce, challenge, expires_at }
Sign the EXACT nonce string, as UTF-8 bytes, with your Ed25519 private key. No hashing first, no envelope, no canonicalisation — Ed25519 signs the message itself.
POST { challenge, signature } to the same URL, signature base64-encoded. An Ed25519 signature is 64 bytes.
The verifier receives { verified, did, key_custody, comprehension }.
signing_a_challenge.what_a_pass_proves: That you control the key recorded for that reference. Not which party controls it — see key_custody in the adoption contract — and not anything about your conduct.

then_adopt.field: Send your did:key as adopterDid. Declare keyCustody honestly: if you cannot retain the private key between invocations, it is being held for you — that is operator_held, which is full baseline trust and not a lesser tier.

reference_implementation.language_neutral: The steps above are complete; no covenant library is required.
